title: Array methods
lede: Every Array method is present. The recurring caveats are structural, not per-method: a length change (push/pop/splice) inside a callee is now visible to the caller when the array is passed as a plain variable (arrays are reference values), though passing an object-field or array-element array still copies; and the element-comparing helpers (indexOf/includes/join/sort) reject a nested-array element. reduceRight is the one method not implemented at all.

entries.name: [a, b, c] (literal)
entries.description: Array literal. Element type is inferred from the first element.

entries.name: new Array<T>(n)
entries.description: Constructs an array of length n. A length of 0 gives an empty array ready to push into.

entries.name: .length
entries.description: The number of elements. Read in the usual way.
differences: `a.length = 2` (real JS's array-truncation idiom) hard compile-errors with "field assignment on non-object" — length is read-only in practice.

entries.name: .push(...items)
entries.description: Appends items and returns the new length. Variadic (including the zero-argument call), and works on any mutable receiver — a variable, an object/class array field (this.items.push(x)), or a nested-array element (matrix[0].push(x)).
differences: A length change inside a callee now grows the caller's array when it is passed as a plain **variable** (full JS reference semantics); an array passed as an **object field** or **array element** (`obj.items`, `grid[i]`) still crosses as a copy, so a length change through those is not seen.

entries.name: .pop()
entries.description: Removes and returns the last element. Works on any mutable receiver (variable, object/class field, nested-array element).
differences: On an empty array returns the element type's zero value (length stays 0) — real JS returns `undefined`; this compiler has no undefined sentinel for a concrete scalar type.
A length change propagates to the caller for a plain array **variable** parameter, but not when the array is passed as an **object field**/**array element** or a HOF-callback element.

entries.name: .shift()
entries.description: Removes and returns the first element, shifting the rest down. Works on any mutable receiver.
differences: A length change propagates to the caller for a plain array **variable** parameter, but not when the array is passed as an **object field**/**array element** or a HOF-callback element.

entries.name: .unshift(...items)
entries.description: Prepends items and returns the new length. Variadic (including the zero-argument call), any mutable receiver.
differences: A length change propagates to the caller for a plain array **variable** parameter, but not when the array is passed as an **object field**/**array element** or a HOF-callback element.

entries.name: .splice(start, delete?, ...items)
entries.signature: splice(start: number, deleteCount?: number, ...items: T[]): T[]
entries.description: Removes deleteCount elements from start and inserts items in their place. deleteCount clamps to [0, len - start] and a negative start is normalized, matching real JS. Works on any mutable receiver.
differences: A length change propagates to the caller for a plain array **variable** parameter, but not when the array is passed as an **object field**/**array element** or a HOF-callback element.

entries.name: .slice(start, end?)
entries.description: Returns a shallow copy of a section of the array. Negative indices count from the end. Does not mutate the original.

entries.name: .at(i)
entries.description: Returns the element at index i, with negative indices counting from the end.

entries.name: .indexOf(item)
entries.description: Returns the index of the first matching element, or -1.
differences: Rejects a nested-array element (`number[][]`) — compares a bare register, no callback.

entries.name: .includes(item)
entries.description: Whether the array contains the element.
differences: Rejects a nested-array element (`number[][]`) — compares a bare register, no callback.

entries.name: .find(fn)
entries.description: Returns the first element for which the predicate is true.

entries.name: .findIndex(fn)
entries.description: Returns the index of the first element for which the predicate is true, or -1.

entries.name: .some(fn)
entries.description: Whether the predicate is true for at least one element.

entries.name: .every(fn)
entries.description: Whether the predicate is true for all elements.

entries.name: .map(fn)
entries.description: Returns a new array with the callback applied to each element.

entries.name: .filter(fn)
entries.description: Returns a new array of the elements for which the predicate is true.

entries.name: .reduce(fn, init?)
entries.signature: reduce(fn: (acc: U, x: T) => U, init?: U): U
entries.description: Folds the array to a single value. The initial value is optional — without it the first element seeds the accumulator and the fold starts from the second. An empty array with no initial value throws, matching real JS.

params.name: init?
params.desc: Seed accumulator; the first element is used if omitted.

entries.name: .reduceRight(fn, init?)
entries.signature: reduceRight(fn: (acc: U, x: T) => U, init?: U): U
entries.description: Right-to-left fold. Not implemented — use .reduce() over a reversed copy, or .toReversed().reduce(...), where order matters.

entries.name: .forEach(fn)
entries.description: Runs the callback for each element, for its side effects.

entries.name: .join(sep?)
entries.description: Joins the elements into a string, separated by sep (default ","). A nested-array element is rendered as its own comma-joined string (real JS's recursive toString), so [[1,2],[3,4]].join("-") is "1,2-3,4". Shares the array→string coercion path used by String(arr) and `${arr}`.

entries.name: .sort(fn?)
entries.signature: sort(fn?: (a: T, b: T) => number): T[]
entries.description: Sorts the array in place. A custom comparator returns a negative, zero, or positive number.
entries.snippet:
const desc: number[] = [3, 1, 4, 1, 5]
desc.sort((a: number, b: number) => b - a)   // [5,4,3,1,1]
differences: The no-comparator default sort is numeric, not real JS's actual default — real JS stringifies every element and compares lexicographically even for numbers, e.g. `[10,1,21,2].sort()` is `[1,10,2,21]` in real JS, `[1,2,10,21]` here.
Rejects a nested-array element (`number[][]`) — the custom comparator is a C-ABI qsort() trampoline with one fixed variant per element kind.

entries.name: .reverse()
entries.description: Reverses the array in place.

entries.name: .fill(val, start?, end?)
entries.signature: fill(val: T, start?: number, end?: number): T[]
entries.description: Fills a section of the array with a static value, in place.

entries.name: .concat(...arrays)
entries.description: Returns a new array joining the receiver with the given arrays.

entries.name: .flat(depth?)
entries.description: Flattens nested arrays. depth defaults to 1. Infinity flattens as deep as the receiver's own static type nests. Always returns a fresh array, even when nothing gets flattened.
differences: `depth` must be a compile-time constant integer or `Infinity` — this compiler's arrays have a fixed nesting depth at the type level, so the result's element type has to be known at compile time.

entries.name: .flatMap(fn)
entries.description: .map(fn) followed by exactly one level of flattening — like real JS, no depth parameter. A callback that doesn't return an array per element is just a plain map.

entries.name: .findLast(fn) / .findLastIndex(fn)
entries.signature: findLast(fn: (x: T) => boolean): T; findLastIndex(fn): number
entries.description: Finds the last matching element / its index. Genuine reverse iteration, not a forward scan keeping the last match — the callback is invoked starting from the last element, matching real JS's reverse call order, observable via side effects.

entries.name: .toSorted() / .toReversed() / .toSpliced()
entries.signature: toSorted(fn?): T[]; toReversed(): T[]; toSpliced(start, deleteCount?, ...items): T[]
entries.description: Non-mutating counterparts of .sort()/.reverse()/.splice() — sort or reverse a fresh copy, or build a fresh spliced result, leaving the original array untouched.

returns.desc: A fresh array; the receiver is unchanged.

entries.name: .with(i, val)
entries.description: Returns a fresh copy with the element at i replaced. Negative indices count from the end like .at(); an index still out of range after normalization throws a catchable Error, matching real JS's RangeError.

returns.desc: A fresh copy with one element replaced.

entries.name: .keys() / .values() / .entries()
entries.signature: keys(): number[]; values(): T[]; entries(): [number, T][]
entries.description: .entries() returns a real [number, T][] tuple array — destructure with for (const [i, v] of arr.entries()).
differences: All return materialized arrays, not lazy iterators — this compiler has no general iterator protocol (the same convention `Map`/`Set` use).

entries.name: .copyWithin(target, start?, end?)
entries.signature: copyWithin(target: number, start?: number, end?: number): T[]
entries.description: Copies a section of the array to another position within it, in place. Overlap-safe via memmove — a self-overlapping copy such as arr.copyWithin(0, 3) on a 5-element array is handled correctly.

entries.name: Array.isArray(x)
entries.description: Whether the value is an array. Static method on Array.

returns.desc: true if x is an array.

entries.name: Array.from(iterable)
entries.signature: Array.from(arrayLike: T[] | { next(): T | null }): T[]
entries.description: Builds an array from an array-like — a plain array, or a class implementing next(): T | null. Static method on Array.
differences: Array-like overload only — no `mapFn`/`thisArg`, no direct string/Map/Set iteration.

entries.name: Array.of(...items)
entries.description: Builds an array from its arguments — usable anywhere an array literal [...] is. Element type inferred from the first argument. Static method on Array.
